summary: Claire Vo interviews Alex Cornell, Meta's design director on Muse, a consumer AI agent app. They discuss design choices (messaging-style chat with an embodied character, a status line with progressive disclosure, a single main chat with optional side chats, proactive messages) and Cornell's personal uses: organizing Instagram saves, a Sky Mall-style shopping feed, monitoring and price-drop triggers, golf and chess dashboards, and a podcast of his old blog. Cornell closes on designing for non-deterministic systems.
speakers_or_authors: Claire Vo (host, How I AI); Alex Cornell (Design Director, Meta Muse)
relevance_reason: Central to the themes: a consumer agent that works in the background, uses personal context (Instagram connector, logged-in sites, memory) and has a conversational, messaging-style interface with design rationale. Evidence is mostly the designer's own account and demos, not independent user data.
themes: Consumer agent design: status, progressive disclosure and latency
Personal context via connectors (Instagram) and memory
Conversational interface as messaging with an entity, single main chat vs threads
Generative UI on the rails: generated artifacts, feeds and avatar states

claims.claim: Muse's design is framed as an exchange with an entity, using messaging patterns (bubbles, embodied character) rather than conventional AI-app conventions. This is partly because the agent can message the user proactively.
Muse shows a status line (working, what it is working on, then a full action list down to raw calls) so non-technical users know it is working without chain-of-thought clutter in the chat.
The host says chain-of-thought UI elements often act as a band-aid for latency. She reports from her own use that Muse's progressive disclosure works and that it is very fast.
Muse acknowledges complex requests with a reaction or initial message, then works in the background and relies on the status display for long tasks.
Generative UI in Muse is bounded. Core surfaces are fixed, but ideas, status emoji and avatar states are generated, and the feed is a native surface rather than a fully generative one.
Cornell had the agent organize his Instagram saves, then render shopping suggestions as a daily Sky Mall-style magazine. He has not connected it to purchasing.
He uses Muse for monitoring (artist releases, concerts, collaborations) and a weekly trigger that checks his wishlist for sales. He also uses it for price comparison and product research.
Agents can log into websites and use connectors like Instagram or Pinterest, making visual personal data usable for design concepts and consolidation, e.g. a manual from hundreds of saved golf tips.
Muse generates recurring dashboards and recaps from his golf and chess data, defined through chat. It also made a morning podcast reading of his old blog recovered from the web.

Muse uses a single canonical main chat with optional side chats, unlike the traditional new-thread-per-conversation model. Cornell says helping users understand the difference is an under-explored area.
Cornell says designing for non-deterministic, highly personal systems means focusing on the underlying architecture and scaffolding rather than each individual screen.
Cornell says his mother uses Muse and apologized to it for making it work so hard, as an anecdote that the app is accessible to non-technical people.

commercial_interest: Cornell is a Meta employee describing Meta's own product, and the host is a self-described big fan. The episode is sponsored by WorkOS (ad read in seg-0003 to seg-0004). There is no independent user data, privacy discussion, or failure/reliability evidence, and the Instagram access is not examined for its privacy trade-off.
older_event: No. The item discusses a current Muse product and its design, not an event older than 30 days. The editor should check separately whether Muse launched recently; the transcript does not say.
